teams.name: Chicago American Giants
teams.fate: Played as Chicago Columbia Giants for 1931 as the NNL collapsed.
teams.note: Won the first NNL pennants in 1920-22 and again in 1926-27.

teams.name: Chicago Columbia Giants
teams.fate: Joined the Negro Southern League as Chicago American Giants in 1932.
teams.note: Renamed for 1931 only; finished last in the incomplete NNL season.

teams.name: Chicago Giants
teams.fate: Dropped from the league after 1921.
teams.note: Traveled without a home field in 1920 and 1921.

teams.name: Cuban Stars (West)
teams.fate: Left the league after 1930 and disbanded.
teams.note: Traveling club; used Redland Field in Cincinnati in 1921 as the Cincinnati Cuban Stars.

teams.name: Dayton Marcos
teams.fate: Dropped after 1920; franchise slot sold to Columbus.

teams.name: Dayton Marcos
teams.fate: Withdrew in July 1926 with a 6-36 record.
teams.note: Rejoined the NNL for a second stint.

teams.name: Detroit Stars
teams.fate: Disbanded when the Negro National League collapsed in 1931.
teams.note: Replaced in 1932 by the Detroit Wolves.

teams.name: Indianapolis ABCs
teams.fate: Folded after the 1926 season; remnants moved to Cleveland.
teams.note: Dropped mid-1924 and returned in 1925 as league membership shifted.

teams.name: Indianapolis ABCs
teams.fate: Moved to the Negro Southern League for 1932.
teams.note: Second Indianapolis club of this name; the 1931 home park was not confirmed.

teams.name: Kansas City Monarchs
teams.fate: Played 1931 as an NNL associate, then went independent in 1932.
teams.note: Won NNL pennants in 1923-25 and 1929.

teams.name: St. Louis Giants
teams.fate: Franchise reorganized and renamed St. Louis Stars for 1922.

teams.name: St. Louis Stars
teams.fate: Folded when the NNL collapsed after the 1931 season.
teams.note: Won NNL pennants in 1928, 1930, and 1931.

teams.name: Columbus Buckeyes
teams.fate: Dissolved after finishing seventh of eight in 1921.
teams.note: Held the former Dayton Marcos franchise slot.

teams.name: Cleveland Tate Stars
teams.fate: Dropped after 1922; returned as 1923 associate, then folded.

teams.name: Pittsburgh Keystones
teams.fate: Disbanded after the 1922 season.

teams.name: Toledo Tigers
teams.fate: Ceased operations in July 1923 with an 11-17 league record.

teams.name: Milwaukee Bears
teams.fate: Disbanded after finishing last in 1923.
teams.note: Played most games on the road because of weak attendance.

teams.name: Cleveland Browns
teams.fate: Disbanded after the 1924 season.
teams.note: Successor to the Tate Stars; played at Hooper Field.

teams.name: Birmingham Black Barons
teams.fate: Left the NNL for the Negro Southern League in 1926.

teams.name: Birmingham Black Barons
teams.fate: Dropped when the NNL shrank in 1931; rejoined the Negro Southern League.

teams.name: Memphis Red Sox
teams.fate: Dropped at the 1926 winter meeting; returned in 1927.
teams.note: Replaced Indianapolis mid-1924.

teams.name: Memphis Red Sox
teams.fate: Withdrew in 1931 to help form the Negro Southern League.

teams.name: Cleveland Elites
teams.fate: Disbanded after failing to finish the second half of 1926.

teams.name: Cleveland Hornets
teams.fate: Disbanded after the 1927 season.
teams.note: Related to the Elites and Tigers; treated here as separate clubs.

teams.name: Cleveland Tigers
teams.fate: Disbanded after finishing 20-59 in 1928.

teams.name: Nashville Elite Giants
teams.fate: Left the NNL after 1930 and joined the Negro Southern League.
teams.note: Franchise later became the Baltimore Elite Giants.

teams.name: Cleveland Cubs
teams.fate: Did not return after finishing second in 1931.
teams.note: Played some games at Hardware Field.

teams.name: Louisville White Sox
teams.fate: Renamed Louisville Black Caps for 1932 in the Negro Southern League.

teams.name: Hilldale Club
teams.fate: Left the ECL after 1927; joined the American Negro League in 1929.
teams.note: Won three ECL pennants.

teams.name: Bacharach Giants
teams.fate: Joined the American Negro League for 1929.

teams.name: Brooklyn Royal Giants
teams.fate: Left the ECL after 1927 and played independently.

teams.name: Cuban Stars (East)
teams.fate: Joined the American Negro League for 1929.
teams.note: Traveling club that used Dyckman Oval and Dexter Park for some home dates.

teams.name: New York Lincoln Giants
teams.fate: Joined the American Negro League for 1929.
teams.note: Played in the 1927 standings despite sources saying they sat out.

teams.name: Baltimore Black Sox
teams.fate: Joined the American Negro League for 1929.

teams.name: Harrisburg Giants
teams.fate: Left the ECL after 1927; most players signed elsewhere.

teams.name: Washington Potomacs
teams.fate: Moved to Wilmington, Delaware, for 1925.
teams.note: Wikipedia names American League Park, a defunct ground; treated as unconfirmed.

teams.name: Wilmington Potomacs
teams.fate: Folded in mid-July 1925; the ECL contracted to seven teams.

teams.name: Newark Stars
teams.fate: Disbanded mid-season after winning one of eleven games.

teams.name: Philadelphia Tigers
teams.fate: Played independently into July after the ECL broke up in June.

teams.name: Bacharach Giants
teams.fate: Original club disbanded after 1929; revived in Philadelphia in 1931.

teams.name: Baltimore Black Sox
teams.fate: League folded after 1929; the club played independently.

teams.name: Cuban Stars (East)
teams.fate: League folded; club continued independently until 1933.

teams.name: Hilldale Club
teams.fate: League folded after 1929; the club played independently.
teams.note: Nicknamed the Darby Daisies from 1929.

teams.name: Homestead Grays
teams.fate: League folded; the Grays returned to independent play.
teams.note: Played home games in Pittsburgh.

teams.name: New York Lincoln Giants
teams.fate: Folded after 1930, as the Depression undid the club.

teams.name: Detroit Wolves
teams.fate: Folded in mid-1932 when owner Cum Posey shut down the league.
teams.note: Played in Hamtramck, Michigan.

teams.name: Homestead Grays
teams.fate: Only survivor of the collapsed East-West League.
teams.note: Wikipedia lists Greenlee Field for 1932; Forbes Field also used in the period.

teams.name: Baltimore Black Sox
teams.fate: Played on after the league folded; disbanded in 1934.

teams.name: Pollock's Cuban Stars
teams.fate: Left the folded league; the club disbanded in 1936.
teams.note: Barnstormed with no home park; also called the Cuban House of David.

teams.name: Newark Browns
teams.fate: Left the league after a few games and continued independently.
teams.note: Played in Bloomfield, New Jersey.

teams.name: Cleveland Stars
teams.fate: Disbanded after finishing 8-16 in 1932.

teams.name: Hilldale Club
teams.fate: Disbanded in July 1932 by owner John Drew.

teams.name: Washington Pilots
teams.fate: Disbanded in 1932 as the East-West League failed.

teams.name: Chicago American Giants
teams.fate: Left the Negro Southern League after its 1932 pennant.
teams.note: Won the 1932 NSL pennant.

teams.name: Monroe Monarchs
teams.fate: Disbanded soon after the mid-1930s.
teams.note: Sources disagree on the club's end date.

teams.name: Birmingham Black Barons
teams.fate: Remained in the Negro Southern League through 1936.

teams.name: Nashville Elite Giants
teams.fate: Continued; later moved to Columbus and Washington before Baltimore.

teams.name: Montgomery Grey Sox
teams.fate: End of the club is not documented in sources consulted.

teams.name: Columbus Turf Club
teams.fate: Folded after the 1932 season.
teams.note: Joined the NSL in July; some sources call it the relocated Louisville club.

teams.name: Indianapolis ABCs
teams.fate: Continued play in later years, moving to other circuits.

teams.name: Memphis Red Sox
teams.fate: Remained a leading Negro league club until 1959.

teams.name: Little Rock Grays
teams.fate: Disbanded during 1932.

teams.name: Atlanta Black Crackers
teams.fate: Continued; moved to Indianapolis after 1938.
teams.note: Shared the park with the white Atlanta Crackers.

teams.name: Louisville Black Caps
teams.fate: Folded in August 1932.
teams.note: Some sources say its remains joined the Columbus Turf Club.

parks.name: South Side Park
parks.status: Demolished; the Wentworth Gardens housing project occupies the site.
notable: Home of the Chicago American Giants from 1911 to 1940.
Hosted the 1926 and 1927 Colored World Series games won by Chicago.
Also hosted the White Sox until 1910 and three 1906 World Series games.

parks.name: Mack Park
parks.status: Demolished in the 1960s; Fairview Homes senior housing now stands on the site.
notable: Detroit Stars home from 1920 through 1929.
A 1929 fire, started while drying the field with gasoline, destroyed the grandstand.
Built by semipro sponsor Joe Roesink at Mack and Fairview Avenues.

parks.name: Hamtramck Stadium
parks.status: Still stands in Veterans Park; renovated and reopened in 2022.
notable: Home of the Detroit Stars in 1930 and the Detroit Wolves in 1932.
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2012.
Ty Cobb threw out the first pitch at the 1930 opening.

parks.name: Association Park
parks.status: Not documented in the sources consulted; coordinates are the city center.
notable: Home of the Kansas City Monarchs from 1920 until mid-1923.
Shared with the minor-league Kansas City Blues.
Wikipedia's Association Park article covers an earlier 1886 park; this is the 1909 ground.

parks.name: Municipal Stadium
parks.status: Demolished in 1976; a municipal garden and housing occupy the site.
notable: Opened as Muehlebach Field in 1923, later Ruppert Stadium and Blues Stadium.
Home of the Monarchs from 1923 to 1955.
Later hosted the Athletics, Royals, and the 1960 All-Star Game.

parks.name: Stars Park
parks.status: Site is now the Harris-Stowe State University baseball field with a Stars Park monument.
notable: Built in 1922 for the St. Louis Stars, one of few parks built for a Negro league club.
Hosted games of the 1925, 1928, and 1930 NNL championship series.
A photograph of the park surfaced only in 2016.

parks.name: Giants Park
parks.status: Industrial area now; coordinates are the city center.
notable: Home of the St. Louis Giants in 1920 and 1921, most games.
Bounded by North Broadway and Clarence and Prescott Avenues.
Renamed Metropolitan Park around 1934.

parks.name: Rickwood Field
parks.status: Still stands as a restored working museum on the National Register.
notable: Called the oldest surviving professional ballpark in the United States.
Shared by the Barons and the Black Barons.
Hosted a 2024 Major League game.

parks.name: Westwood Field
parks.status: Site not documented in the sources consulted; coordinates are the city center.
notable: Home of the Dayton Marcos in 1920 and 1926.
Opened as West Side Park; Marcos opened their 1920 NNL home slate here.

parks.name: Neil Park
parks.status: Not documented in the sources consulted; coordinates are the city center.
notable: Home of the Columbus Buckeyes in their 1921 NNL season.
Retrosheet lists 1921 NNL games here.

parks.name: Tate Field
parks.status: Now a golf course; coordinates are the city center.
notable: Home of the Tate Stars in 1922 and later the Browns, Elites, and Hornets.
Renamed Hooper Field; Beyerle and Sykora Roads bounded it.

parks.name: Luna Park
parks.status: Housing now covers the site; coordinates are the city center.
notable: Ballpark inside an amusement park.
Home of the 1928 Cleveland Tigers.

parks.name: Cleveland Hardware Field
parks.status: Housing now covers the site; coordinates are the city center.
notable: At East 79th Street and Kinsman Road.
Used by the 1931 Cubs and the 1932 Cleveland Stars.

parks.name: Central Park
parks.status: Now a public park in the Hill District.
notable: First black-owned and black-managed ballpark in Pittsburgh.
Designed by Louis Bellinger, later architect of Greenlee Field.
Home of the Pittsburgh Keystones in 1921 and 1922.

parks.name: Forbes Field
parks.status: Partly remembered on the University of Pittsburgh campus; left-center wall segment still stands.
notable: First steel-and-concrete ballpark in the National League.
Bill Mazeroski's 1960 Game 7 home run ended the World Series here.
Used by the Homestead Grays in the late 1920s and 1930s.

parks.name: Greenlee Field
parks.status: The Bedford Dwellings housing project occupies the site.
notable: Black-owned park built for Gus Greenlee's Crawfords in 1932.
Homestead Grays also used it from 1932 to 1937.
Satchel Paige pitched to Josh Gibson at the opening.

parks.name: Swayne Field
parks.status: Shopping center now stands; part of the left-field wall remains.
notable: Home of the Toledo Mud Hens from 1909 to 1955.
Toledo Tigers played their 1923 NNL season here.
Named for donor Noah Swayne Jr.

parks.name: Borchert Field
parks.status: Demolished in the 1950s; Interstate 43 now runs over the site.
notable: Called Athletic Park until the late 1920s.
Milwaukee Bears played their only NNL season here in 1923.
Also hosted early Green Bay Packers games.

parks.name: Martin Stadium
parks.status: Demolished in 1961; a semi-truck dealership stands there with a historical marker.
notable: Built in 1923 by R. S. Lewis as Lewis Park for the Red Sox.
Renamed for the Martin brothers after their 1927 purchase.
Expanded in 1947 at a cost of $200,000.

parks.name: Tom Wilson Park
parks.status: Demolished; site not further described in sources.
notable: Built by owner Tom Wilson for the Nashville Elite Giants.
One of three Negro league parks built for a specific team.
Hosted spring training for Negro and minor league clubs.

parks.name: Washington Park
parks.status: Mostly covered by the Indianapolis Zoo; a marker was placed in 2011.
notable: Home of the Indianapolis ABCs from 1920 to 1926.
Enlarged to about 20,000 seats after a 1909 rebuild.
Said to be the largest field in the minor leagues.

parks.name: Bush Stadium
parks.status: Converted into the Stadium Lofts apartments; light towers still stand.
notable: Opened in 1931 as Perry Stadium, later Victory Field.
Indianapolis ABCs played here in 1932, 1938, and 1939.
Its ivy inspired the ivy at Wrigley Field.

parks.name: Parkway Field
parks.status: Site is an intramural field near the University of Louisville; the diamond is gone.
notable: Home of the Louisville Black Caps from 1930 to 1932.
Used by Louisville Colonels from 1923 into the 1950s.
Center field ran about 512 feet in 1936.

parks.name: Hilldale Park
parks.status: Retail stores and parking lots; a Pennsylvania historical marker stands there.
notable: Home of the Hilldale Club from 1910 to 1932.
A tree in center field was treated as in play.
Site of the 1925 Negro League World Series games.

parks.name: Bacharach Park
parks.status: Carver Hall Apartments now occupy the site.
notable: Named for Atlantic City mayor Harry Bacharach, as were the Giants.
Right field was unusually shallow to fit a city block.
Hosted games in the 1926 and 1927 Colored World Series.

parks.name: Atlantic Park Dog Track
parks.status: Not documented in the sources consulted; coordinates are the city center.
notable: Greyhound track used by the Bacharach Giants as home in 1928 and 1929.

parks.name: Maryland Baseball Park
parks.status: Site of the Wheelabrator Baltimore plant.
notable: Home of the Baltimore Black Sox in the 1920s.
Stood about half a mile north of Westport Park.

parks.name: Bugle Field
parks.status: Vacant lot after an industrial plant; coordinates are the city center.
notable: Owned by Joe Cambria, who added lights for night games.
Black Sox moved here in 1932; the Elite Giants later used it.

parks.name: Dexter Park
parks.status: Redeveloped with houses and a supermarket in the late 1950s.
notable: Home of the Brooklyn Royal Giants from 1923 to 1931.
Installed New York City's first permanent baseball lights in 1930.
Located in Woodhaven near the Brooklyn border.

parks.name: Catholic Protectory Oval
parks.status: Not documented in the sources consulted; coordinates are in the Bronx.
notable: Home of the Lincoln Giants from 1920 to 1930.
Located in the Bronx.

parks.name: Island Park
parks.status: On City Island; ballfield later reused for baseball.
notable: Home of the Harrisburg Giants from 1922 to 1927.
The Giants also played Sundays at Rossmere Park in Lancaster.

parks.name: Harlan Field
parks.status: Not documented in the sources consulted; coordinates are the city center.
notable: Listed as the 1925 home of the Wilmington Potomacs.

parks.name: Ruppert Stadium
parks.status: Not documented in the sources consulted; coordinates are the city center.
notable: Opened as Davids' Stadium; the Newark Stars played here in 1926.

parks.name: Pencoyd Field
parks.status: Not documented in the sources consulted; coordinates are near Wissahickon station.
notable: Home of the 1928 Philadelphia Tigers in Manayunk.

parks.name: General Electric Field
parks.status: Not documented in the sources consulted; coordinates are the city center.
notable: Home of the 1932 Newark Browns of the East-West League.

parks.name: Griffith Stadium
parks.status: Demolished in 1965; Howard University Hospital now occupies the site.
notable: Home of the Washington Senators from 1911 to 1960.
Hosted the 1940 NFL championship, a 73-0 Bears win.
Hosted the 1937 and 1956 All-Star Games.

parks.name: Ponce de Leon Park
parks.status: A strip mall stood here, later demolished; the magnolia tree remains.
notable: A center-field magnolia kept balls in play until the wall moved in 1947.
Atlanta Black Crackers shared the park with the white Crackers.
Hosted Atlanta's first integrated crowd in 1962.

parks.name: Crump Park
parks.status: Not documented in the sources consulted; coordinates are the city center.
notable: Home of the 1932 Little Rock Grays.

parks.name: Casino Park
parks.status: Not documented in the sources consulted; coordinates are the city center.
notable: Home of the Monroe Monarchs near 29th and Hope.
A white Monroe Twins team leased it in 1937.

parks.name: Cramton Bowl
parks.status: Still stands as a football stadium.
notable: Hosted the South's first night football game in 1927.
Montgomery Grey Sox played here in 1932.
